title: One window. Three moods. A product photography exercise.
excerpt: A bottle, a window and two pieces of card: a practical way to change the feeling of a product photograph before reaching for a preset.
coverAlt: Concept still life of a cobalt bottle, directional window light and a warm shadow.
body:
A small lighting setup can produce a surprisingly wide range of images. The useful question is not how many lights are available, but what the light needs to say about the object. A quiet ceramic cup, a bright drink bottle and a precise metal tool should not all feel identical.

This exercise uses one object, one window, a white card and a dark card. Keep the camera position fixed for the first round. That constraint makes changes in shadow and reflection easier to understand. The cover is an AI-generated editorial illustration of the idea, rather than documentation of a completed client shoot.

# Begin with a light map

Place the product beside the window, away from direct sun if the contrast is too harsh. Before taking a photograph, walk around it. Notice where its outline disappears, which surfaces reflect the window and where the shadow falls. Choose a camera position that explains the product's shape. Clean visible dust now; retouching should not become a substitute for looking carefully.

Make a reference frame with no cards. Keep exposure and white balance consistent while comparing the first variations. Otherwise, a change in brightness can disguise what moving a card actually did.

# Mood one: open and approachable

Hold the white card on the shadow side, outside the frame. Bring it closer until the dark side becomes readable without flattening the object. Leave a small difference between the lit and shaded surfaces. That difference gives the product volume. A light surface and some breathing room can make this version useful for a clear introductory image.

# Mood two: sculpted and deliberate

Replace the white card with the dark one. Move it slowly and watch the edge of the product rather than the whole frame. The aim is a controlled dark reflection or deeper shadow that describes the form. If the object becomes a silhouette, pull the card back. More darkness does not automatically mean more sophistication.

# Mood three: energetic and graphic

Rotate the entire setup so the window light crosses the scene at a different angle. Let a diagonal shadow become part of the composition. Leave a usable area for a headline, but do not add text yet. First decide whether the photograph has a strong enough visual structure without it. Avoid a shadow that hides a label or an important product detail.

# Compare intent, not just brightness

Put the three frames beside one another. For each, write a single sentence: welcoming, sculptural or energetic. Ask whether the photograph supports that sentence at thumbnail size. Then check the label, outline and surface detail at full size.

Finish by choosing one frame for each purpose instead of forcing one edit to serve every placement. Save a simple setup note: product position, window direction, card position and camera height. A repeatable observation is more valuable than an effect that cannot be rebuilt.
author: Rajneesh Vaishnav

title: Photographing glass: make the edges do the talking.
excerpt: Transparent objects need something to reflect. Build cleaner glass photographs by shaping the surroundings instead of simply adding more brightness.
coverAlt: AI-generated glass still life with cobalt edges, clear vessels and coral reflections.
body:
A glass object can look empty in a photograph even when the exposure is technically comfortable. Its shape is partly described by what surrounds it: bright areas, dark areas and the transitions between them. If those surroundings are unplanned, the glass can become a collection of distracting reflections.

Treat the space around the object as part of the set. This approach works as a learning exercise for drinking glasses, perfume-style bottles and other transparent props. The editorial cover is a generated concept; use your own test frames to judge how a real material behaves.

# Design the outline first

Start with one clean object on a stable surface. Put a simple background behind it and make the first frame without decorative props. Look at the rim, sides and base. Can each be separated from the background? If not, move a dark or light card beside the object, outside the crop, and observe the reflection it creates.

Make one adjustment at a time. A card shifted a small distance may change an entire edge. Photographing every small adjustment is useful because the eye quickly adapts to the latest version and forgets the previous one.

# Separate reflections from distractions

Not every reflection needs to disappear. A long highlight can explain a curved surface; a random bright rectangle can make it look damaged. Decide which marks describe the object and which belong to the room. Change the room before trying to erase every problem in Photoshop.

Check for a reflected camera, a bright shirt or a cluttered shelf. Repositioning the camera or simplifying the area near it may solve the problem more cleanly than adding another light. Keep the product's front details readable while doing this.

# Give the base a reason to exist

A transparent object still needs to feel grounded. A controlled shadow, a subtle reflection or a change in surface texture can help. Avoid letting a dramatic base reflection compete with the actual rim and body. If the tabletop is becoming the main subject, simplify it.

For an advertising image, try placing a small piece of coloured paper outside the frame. Its reflection can introduce a brand colour without colouring the entire scene. Compare that version with a neutral reference so the material does not accidentally appear to be a different colour.

# Retouch without inventing a new material

Clean dust and temporary marks, but preserve useful tonal transitions. Removing every irregularity can leave glass looking like smooth plastic. Work with the reference frame open beside the retouch. Ask whether the outline, thickness and transparency still agree with the object you photographed.

# A final three-size check

Review the image at full size for marks, at normal page size for shape and at thumbnail size for recognition. A beautiful highlight that only works when enlarged may not help an e-commerce grid. Keep a clear descriptive image alongside the more expressive advertising version. They have different jobs, and both can belong in a considered product story.
author: Rajneesh Vaishnav

title: The nine-frame product story: plan a shoot beyond the hero image.
excerpt: Build a small, purposeful image sequence that answers a buyer’s questions instead of delivering nine near-identical angles.
coverAlt: Generated contact-sheet concept showing a terracotta vessel from different viewpoints.
body:
A hero photograph earns attention. The rest of a product sequence has to explain what that attention is for. When every frame repeats the same angle with a different prop, the gallery gets longer without becoming more useful.

Plan a nine-frame story around questions a viewer might ask. This is a flexible planning exercise, not a rule that every product needs exactly nine images. A simple object may need fewer; a complex one may need more. The generated cover visualises a planning board rather than a real product catalogue.

# Frames one to three: recognise the object

Frame one is the invitation: a composed hero with a clear subject. Frame two is a plain, descriptive view that gives the product less to hide behind. Frame three shows its opposite side or another angle that changes understanding. If the third frame repeats the second, replace it with something useful.

Keep scale and product colour consistent. A buyer should not wonder whether the images show different versions because the lighting changed dramatically between frames. Write down which details must remain visible in every key view.

# Frames four to six: answer practical questions

Frame four explains scale using a credible context, such as a hand holding a cup. Frame five isolates a relevant detail: a closure, edge, surface or connection. Frame six shows an actual interaction. The interaction must match what the product can really do.

Do not invent dimensions, performance claims or accessories to fill a layout. If a detail needs a written explanation, request verified product information before designing the callout. A confident layout cannot make an unsupported statement accurate.

# Frames seven to nine: add context and distinction

Frame seven places the object in a believable environment. Frame eight focuses on a material or crafted detail. Frame nine closes the sequence with another reason to remember it: an alternate arrangement, a packaging view or a calm composition that brings the visual language together.

These roles can change. A package that contains several parts may need an included-items photograph much earlier. A piece of jewellery may need a closer scale reference. Let the buyer's uncertainty determine the order.

# Turn the list into a practical shoot plan

Group frames by setup, not by final gallery order. Photograph all clean views under the same lighting before building the more elaborate context. Prepare surfaces, props and a neutral reference. Leave room around each subject for the intended crops, and make one safety frame with extra space.

After the shoot, name files by purpose rather than by enthusiasm: hero, front, reverse, scale, detail, interaction, context, material and closing. This makes the sequence easier to discuss with a client.

# Edit the sequence as a whole

Lay out the nine frames at equal thumbnail size. Remove anything that answers no new question. Look for changes in colour, scale and contrast that feel accidental. The strongest sequence is not necessarily the one with the most dramatic individual images. It is the one that keeps attention while making the product easier to understand.
author: Rajneesh Vaishnav

title: Before you add another effect, fix the hierarchy.
excerpt: A practical poster audit using one message, three levels of type and a deliberate path through the page.
coverAlt: Abstract editorial typography sculpture with cobalt letterforms, cream paper and coral accents.
body:
A crowded design often asks for another effect when it actually needs a decision. A new shadow, gradient or sticker may make the page feel busier without clarifying its message. Hierarchy starts by deciding what deserves attention first, what supports it and what can wait.

Use a fictional launch poster for this exercise. Give it one main promise, one supporting sentence and one action. Keep the copy short enough that you can judge the layout rather than spend the whole session rewriting it. The cover is a generated editorial illustration, not an example of finished client typography.

# Decide the first thing someone should remember

Write the main message on a separate sheet. If the poster contains six equally important claims, choose the one that makes the others worth reading. Put that message into the layout without an image. Use size, position and available space to establish its role before adding colour.

Now look away and glance back. What do you see first? If the date or decorative badge wins by accident, adjust the structure. The intended reading order should survive before the final artwork is introduced.

# Build three distinct levels

Give the headline, supporting copy and practical details recognisably different roles. That does not require three typefaces. A display family and a readable supporting family can produce plenty of variation through size, weight and placement.

Try the hierarchy in monochrome. If everything merges into one grey block, the relationship between levels needs more work. If one word is enormous but says nothing useful, size alone has not solved the message.

# Use alignment as a quiet organising tool

Choose a small number of shared edges. The headline, paragraph and action can feel related even when they occupy different parts of the page. Arbitrary near-alignments often look like mistakes: either make the relationship precise or separate the elements confidently.

In Figma, build the text groups so changes to the supporting copy do not break the whole composition. In Photoshop, keep editable text and related elements organised. The application is less important than making the design easy to revise.

# Let the image join the hierarchy

Add the main visual after the reading order works. It can frame the message, interrupt a predictable rhythm or create a deliberate focal point. It should not make essential words unreadable. Check contrast where actual text sits, rather than judging the background colour in isolation.

Reserve your strongest accent for a meaningful purpose. If every badge, underline and button uses the same loud treatment, the accent stops directing attention.

# Test the design away from the canvas

View it at the size someone will actually encounter: a phone feed, a presentation slide or a printed sheet. Read it without zooming. Ask another person what they remember after a short look, without explaining the intended answer.

Only then consider an additional effect. Keep it if it strengthens the message or the visual character. Remove it if its main contribution is proving that another tool was used. A deliberate hierarchy makes creative detail more visible because it gives that detail somewhere to belong.
author: Rajneesh Vaishnav

title: One campaign, three formats: redesign the crop, not the idea.
excerpt: How to carry one visual idea across a poster, square social post and wide banner without shrinking the entire design.
coverAlt: Generated paper-format study with coordinated portrait, square and landscape compositions.
body:
A campaign can look coherent across several formats without using the same composition everywhere. The idea stays recognisable; the arrangement responds to the space. Trouble begins when a tall poster is simply reduced to fit a wide banner, leaving the message small and the edges full of unused space.

Build a small campaign around a fictional object or event. Make a portrait poster, a square social post and a landscape banner. Treat these as three related designs, not three exports of the same flattened file. The generated cover illustrates this relationship with abstract paper compositions.

# Separate the identity from the arrangement

Write down the elements that should stay consistent: the main message, type pairing, colour relationships, image treatment and tone of the action. Then identify what can move: the crop, line breaks, spacing, image scale and position of supporting information.

This distinction makes feedback easier. A client can recognise the campaign even when the product moves from the centre of a poster to one side of a banner. Consistency becomes a set of decisions rather than a demand for identical coordinates.

# Build the widest and narrowest versions early

Do not perfect the square version and discover later that the idea cannot survive a banner. Sketch the extreme formats first. In a tall composition, the headline and image can stack. In a wide one, they may need to share the horizontal space. Leave room for a useful crop before committing to intricate details.

A useful test is to place the three rough layouts together before applying final effects. If one format looks like a different campaign, find the missing connection. If one feels cramped, shorten or reorganise its supporting copy instead of making everything tiny.

# Keep the source editable

In Photoshop, preserve the subject, shadows, text and supporting graphics on separate, sensibly named layers. In Figma, use organised frames and reusable styles for the parts that genuinely repeat. In Canva, keep a clear master reference and review each resized version manually.

A layout tool can preserve positions without preserving meaning. Always inspect a generated resize. Check whether the headline still has a natural break, the subject has enough room and the action remains visible.

# Choose a crop with a job

A close crop can make a square post feel immediate. A wider crop can let the banner explain context. Avoid cutting through a feature that identifies the product or through an important part of a person's face or gesture. When the existing photograph cannot support a format, use a different approved image rather than forcing the crop.

# Review a real-size family

Export test files and view them at realistic display sizes. Check text contrast, subject recognition and the distance between essential content and the edges. Keep important details clear of any known platform overlays for the placement.

The final family should feel related when seen together and complete when seen alone. That is the difference between a campaign system and a collection of resized rectangles: each piece carries the same idea with a composition that belongs to its own space.
author: Rajneesh Vaishnav

title: A logo is only the beginning: give a visual identity somewhere to live.
excerpt: Test a brand idea on real applications before calling the identity finished. A practical route from a memorable mark to a usable visual system.
coverAlt: AI-generated identity concept with a coral folded symbol, cobalt sleeve and embossed paper.
body:
A logo presentation can be impressive while leaving the most important design questions unanswered. What does the brand look like when the symbol is tiny? What happens when there is no room for the full name? How does the identity behave on packaging, a social post or a simple invoice?

A visual identity becomes useful when its decisions survive those ordinary conditions. Build applications early enough that they can challenge the mark. The cover is an AI-generated fictional identity concept, not a claim about a commissioned brand or an existing trademark.

# Start with a brand sentence

Describe what the brand does, who it serves and the quality it should communicate. Keep the sentence concrete. A repair workshop that values clarity needs a different visual argument from a theatrical fashion label, even if both ask for something premium.

Translate the sentence into a few design criteria. For example: legible at small size, confident without being aggressive and recognisable in one colour. Use those criteria to evaluate sketches rather than relying only on personal preference.

# Make the mark work in plain conditions

Before adding a material effect, examine the silhouette and the space inside it. Reduce it. Reverse it. Print it simply. If an important idea disappears, decide whether the mark needs refinement or a separate small-size version. A beautiful three-dimensional rendering cannot repair a confused underlying shape.

This does not mean every identity must look minimal. Detailed marks can be expressive, but they still need a practical version for constrained uses. Let the character of the brand determine the level of detail, then design the supporting system around that choice.

# Build three revealing applications

Choose applications that expose different problems. A small avatar tests recognition. A piece of packaging tests hierarchy and material. A social post tests whether the brand can communicate when the logo is not the dominant element.

Use plausible content lengths rather than placing only a short brand name everywhere. A system that works with five letters may struggle with a product description, a price and an instruction. Find that weakness before the final presentation.

# Decide what repeats

Document a small set of useful relationships: colours, display and body type, spacing, image treatment and the role of a graphic motif. Explain where variation is welcome. A template can be recognisable without making every post look mechanically identical.

Keep examples of both a quiet layout and a louder one. This helps show whether the identity has range while remaining coherent. Avoid inventing dozens of rules that nobody needs to use.

# Deliver clarity with the artwork

Name the files clearly and separate production assets from presentation mockups. Explain which version belongs on light or dark backgrounds and which is intended for small uses. Include any necessary licensing information for fonts and supplied assets.

For a concept portfolio, label speculative work honestly. For commercial use, the client also needs appropriate checks on the proposed name and mark. A strong identity presentation shows imagination and responsibility together: an idea worth remembering, and a system someone can actually use.
author: Rajneesh Vaishnav

title: AI art direction starts before the prompt.
excerpt: Turn a vague request into a specific visual brief before generating images. A practical framework for more intentional campaign concepts.
coverAlt: Surreal generated citrus campaign concept with a cobalt architectural wave and coral light.
body:
An image generator can supply visual possibilities quickly. It cannot decide which possibility serves a client's purpose unless that purpose is made clear. Starting with a long list of style adjectives often produces a polished image with no strong reason to exist.

Begin with a short visual brief. The aim is not to find a magic prompt. It is to make decisions that can guide generation, selection and finishing. The cover is an AI-generated campaign-style illustration for a fictional visual exercise, not an actual product advertisement.

# Give the image one job

Write the intended audience, placement and main message. A banner that introduces a new product has a different job from a technical detail image. Decide what the viewer should notice first and what should become clear after a closer look.

Then describe the feeling in terms that can be seen. Instead of only writing energetic, specify a diagonal composition, a clear focal point and a controlled colour contrast. Instead of premium, describe the material, lighting and amount of visual space. Make the abstract preference actionable.

# Define the parts that cannot drift

List product characteristics, approved brand colours, required space for copy and details that must remain accurate. If a real package is involved, keep the approved artwork as a separate production asset. Do not assume generated packaging text will reproduce it correctly.

Also write an avoid list based on the brief. It might include duplicate objects, an impossible closure, misleading ingredients or a setting that changes the meaning of the product. Useful constraints come from the project, not from a generic collection of negative words.

# Explore genuinely different directions

Create a small set of concepts that differ in their visual logic: one might use material contrast, another scale and another environment. Changing only the background colour is a variation, but it is not necessarily a new idea.

Compare concepts against the same brief. Which makes the subject readable? Which leaves room for the actual headline? Which introduces a visual story that can continue into other campaign assets? Select with reasons rather than saving the most surprising image automatically.

# Finish in a design environment

Bring the selected image into Photoshop or another appropriate editor. Correct visible errors, refine the crop and combine it with approved artwork. Set the headline and practical information as editable type in the layout tool. Check that the finished composition works at its intended size.

Generation and layout are separate decisions. A dramatic image can still be a poor banner if the message has nowhere to sit.

# Keep a short decision record

Save the brief, selected prompt, source references and finishing notes. Label generated concept work clearly in a portfolio. When a result succeeds, explain the design decision that made it useful instead of presenting the tool as the entire process.

The most persuasive AI design work shows judgment from beginning to end. It connects an idea, an audience and a final composition. The prompt is part of that process; the direction begins before it and the responsibility continues after it.
author: Rajneesh Vaishnav

title: Build a character system, not thirteen unrelated portraits.
excerpt: Use a clear reference sheet, a controlled wardrobe and a review checklist to make character variations feel like one person.
coverAlt: Generated character reference sheet with a fictional adult woman in consistent cobalt clothing.
body:
A character series can share an illustration style while quietly changing the person in every image. Eye shape drifts, a jacket gains a new collar and the face becomes younger or older. These shifts are easy to miss when each image is judged on its own.

Treat a recurring character as a small design system. Establish the identity before asking for many scenes. This approach does not guarantee perfect consistency from a generator, but it makes inconsistency easier to recognise and correct. The cover is a generated reference-sheet concept for a fictional adult character.

# Write a useful character brief

Describe the character's role, approximate age, silhouette, hairstyle, clothing and a few distinctive visual features. Keep the description focused. A long biography will not necessarily help if the face, proportions and wardrobe remain vague.

Choose which features are fixed and which can change. An outfit may change between stories; a signature hairstyle might not. Decide this deliberately so an intentional variation does not get confused with an error.

# Establish a neutral reference

Begin with a clear front view, a three-quarter view and a profile. Use simple lighting and a quiet expression. Add a full-body view if the character will appear in wider scenes. A highly dramatic pose can be memorable but makes a poor sole reference for everyday proportions.

Review these views together before producing a larger set. If they already look like different people, resolve that first. Select the most reliable reference and keep it available when generating later variations, where the chosen tool supports reference inputs.

# Change one dimension at a time

Test expression without changing wardrobe, location and lighting simultaneously. Then test pose. Then introduce environments. This controlled sequence helps identify what causes the identity to drift.

Keep rejected outputs separate from approved references. Otherwise, an attractive but inconsistent image can accidentally become the basis for the next round. A small approved set is more useful than a large folder with no clear decisions.

# Review the unglamorous details

Check facial proportions, hairline, ear placement, clothing construction and recurring accessories. Compare hands and body proportions as well as the face. A close-up can hide inconsistencies that become obvious when the character is shown full length.

View the entire series as thumbnails, then inspect selected areas at full size. Thumbnail comparison reveals changes in silhouette and age; close inspection reveals surface and structural errors. Correct the image or regenerate the relevant variation instead of explaining away a visible mismatch.

# Present the story clearly

Give each character a separate folder and choose a cover that represents the approved identity. A landscape reference sheet can work better than a portrait when several views need to be visible. Keep the full images available inside the folder so the viewer can inspect them properly.

For portfolio presentation, distinguish generated concepts from commissioned character work. Explain the constraints and the review process. The creative value is not the number of portraits produced; it is the quality of the character decisions and the care taken to make the series belong together.
author: Rajneesh Vaishnav

title: Beautiful is not enough: a credibility check for AI product visuals.
excerpt: A close inspection of structure, materials, copy and claims before a generated concept enters a product layout.
coverAlt: Generated precision still life of a brushed-metal kettle, tactile details and material samples.
body:
A generated product image can look convincing at a glance and become confusing under inspection. A spout may merge into a handle, reflections can imply the wrong material and tiny packaging text may suggest information that nobody approved.

Before using the image in a layout, review it as a product representation rather than only as a picture. The cover is a generated fictional design study. It is not evidence that the pictured object exists or performs in a particular way.

# Inspect structure before surface polish

Trace the silhouette slowly. Check how parts connect, where openings begin and whether the object could plausibly be assembled. Look for duplicated controls, inconsistent seams and handles that attach differently from one side to the other.

Compare the result with approved product references when a real item is being represented. A small structural change may matter much more than a beautiful reflection. If accuracy is central to the placement, an actual photograph may be the appropriate source rather than a generated substitute.

# Ask what each material is doing

Metal, glass, paper and fabric have different visual behaviours. Check whether a reflection follows the surface, whether a transparent area reveals something plausible and whether texture changes unexpectedly across connected parts.

Do not remove every irregularity automatically. Some surface variation helps an image feel tactile. The question is whether it describes a coherent material or hides an unresolved generation error. Keep a neutral reference view beside the more expressive concept during the finishing stage.

# Separate decorative ideas from factual claims

A floating botanical element may communicate a mood, but it can also imply an ingredient. A badge can look like a certification even when it was added only for visual balance. Treat both as meaning, not harmless decoration.

Use only verified claims and approved labels in commercial artwork. Avoid invented dimensions, ingredients, performance figures or awards. A concept portfolio can still be imaginative if it clearly identifies a fictional product and keeps the writing descriptive rather than pretending to report tested performance.

# Rebuild essential typography

Set product names, body copy and callouts as editable text in Photoshop, Figma or the chosen layout application. Check spelling, hierarchy and contrast at realistic display size. Do not leave convincing-looking generated microtext where the viewer expects factual information.

If approved packaging artwork exists, place and review that artwork carefully. Inspect perspective, boundaries and legibility. A correctly spelled label can still look pasted on if its relationship to the surface is wrong.

# Review the finished layout at three distances

At thumbnail size, check the subject and message. At normal size, check hierarchy and material. At full size, inspect details and cleanup. Ask whether any visual treatment could mislead someone about the actual item.

Keep notes on what was generated, what was edited and which references were used. Label portfolio concepts accordingly. A strong final image can be both inventive and clear about its status. That clarity protects the meaning of the work and helps clients understand the judgment behind it.
author: Rajneesh Vaishnav
